item.title: Dutch men face Argentina in World Cup hockey, women win again
item.description:
Dutch men face Argentina in World Cup hockey, women win again

August 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch men’s hockey team are taking on Argentina in their second World Cup group match on Tuesday, with the winners set to take a giant step towards the knock-out rounds.

Both teams won their opening matches comfortably, with the Netherlands beating New Zealand 5-1 in Amstelveen while Argentina overcame Japan by a 3-0 scoreline at the same venue.

The Netherlands and Belgium are co-hosting the tournament, 12 years after the World Cup was held in The Hague. On that occasion the Dutch women’s team won their tournament while the men lost in the final to Australia.

The women’s team are on the brink of reaching the quarter-finals this time after coming through a tricky tie against Australia to win 4-2.

Goalkeeper Anne Veenendaal was kept busy in the opening period as the Dutch had to defend seven penalty corners before taking the lead when Yibbi Jansen scored from a penalty corner at the other end.

Joosje Burg made it two midway through the second period, but Australia hit back almost immediately through Stephanie Kershaw.

After a goalless third quarter, the Australians equalised when Abigail Wilson converted a penalty corner, but Burg restored the lead with her second before Marijn Veen rounded off a fine move to make sure of the points.

In an intriguing subplot, the Argentinian men’s team includes Nicolas Keenan, the fiancé of Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by hockey.nl (@hockeynl)


Jetten wore an Argentina replica shirt as he cheered on his partner from the sidelines on Sunday’s match, but was evasive when asked by RTL which team he would be supporting on Tuesday.

“Hopefully it’ll be a draw so we don’t have to fall out at home,” he joked.

item.title: More Dutch adults are single or living apart, says CBS
item.description:
More Dutch adults are single or living apart, says CBS

August 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The amount of people in the Netherlands who are single is rising, and a growing number are in relationships with a partner they do not live with, new figures from statistics agency CBS show.

In 2025, 30% of adults said they had no long-term partner, up from 27% in 2013. A further 10% were in a so-called “living apart together” relationship – a couple who keep separate homes – compared with 8% in 2013. The remaining 60% lived with a partner.

At the start of 2025, 5.7 million adults did not live with a partner. Most of them, 4.4 million, were living alone, while 627,000 were single parents and others still lived with their own parents.

Single women happier
Single women were more likely to call themselves happy (82%) than single men (76%), the agency found. People in couples were happier still: 92% of those living with a partner said they were happy, whether married or not.

Women were slightly more likely to be single overall (32%) than men (28%). Among the under-25s, most were single (62%) or living apart from a partner (29%), and just 8% shared a home with one.

The pattern shifts with age. From 45 onwards single women outnumber single men, an effect CBS links partly to divorce, after which men more often find a new partner. Among divorced women, 68% were single, against 55% of divorced men.

By 75 and over, about 42% of people lived alone with no partner, mostly because a partner had died. Just over half were still living with someone.

item.title: Schools return as new Dutch and maths targets become law
item.description:
Schools return as new Dutch and maths targets become law

August 17, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Schools in the north of the Netherlands are the first to go back after the summer holidays, and they return to a new set of legally binding targets for what pupils have to learn in Dutch and maths.

The updated core curriculum objectives (kerndoelen) were written into law this month for the first time, NOS reported on Monday. They set out the knowledge and skills pupils are expected to acquire in primary school and the first years of secondary education.

The previous objectives dated from 2006 and were criticised as out of date, vague, and non-committal. There are now fewer of them for Dutch, but what pupils should be able to do is described more concretely. Literature has a clearly defined role, and language development is to be built into other subjects as well.

Junior education minister Judith Tielen said the change was needed because of a serious decline in basic language and maths skills.

Falling standards
The Netherlands was previously seen internationally as one of the leaders in reading, but standards have dropped sharply in recent years.

Tielen wrote to MPs recently that no other European country has seen learning performance fall as far, and school inspectors have found year after year that many children cannot read, write, or do basic maths at the expected level.

Earlier attempts to turn this around – a masterplan on basic skills launched in 2022 and the national programme set up to make up for learning lost during the coronavirus closures – have not had the intended effect, Tielen said. She is working on a new approach prioritising language.

The objectives for the remaining subjects, including two new ones – digital literacy and citizenship – are due to be made law next summer. Schools have until 2031 to incorporate all of them into their teaching.

Ilja Cornelisz, an education researcher at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam, said ambitious objectives do matter because basic skills are under pressure, but that more is needed to improve schooling.

The real task, he said, is giving teachers the professional room, the reliable knowledge, and the support to deliver the goals in their own classrooms, while leaving schools free to decide how they get there.

item.title: Two minors held after second Zaandam explosion in five days
item.description:
Two minors held after second Zaandam explosion in five days

August 17, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Police have arrested two minors on suspicion of involvement in an explosion that blew the back wall off a Zaandam flat in the early hours of Monday.

The blast at the Hof van Zaenden was reported at about 1.40am and was followed by a fire, which the fire service put out quickly. Residents of the block were evacuated because of fears it might collapse, regional broadcaster NH reported.

Nobody was in the flat where the device went off and no one was hurt by the blast, police said.

Officers found the two suspects in a car close to the block shortly after the explosion. Police have not given their ages, saying only that both are under 18.

Debris from the wall was scattered on both sides of the building, and windows and frames in neighbouring flats were damaged. Forensic officers worked with the defence ministry’s bomb disposal unit to secure evidence at the scene.

It is the second explosion in Zaandam in five days. A blast damaged a window at a house on Saenredamstraat late on Thursday, and police are still appealing for witnesses.

item.title: The IamExpat Fair is back in Eindhoven: what’s new this year?
item.description:
Partner content

The IamExpat Fair is back in Eindhoven: what’s new this year?

August 17, 2026

The IamExpat Fair returns to Eindhoven on Saturday October 3 for its second outing in the city, with a bigger careers section, two international centres and a new kids area.

The fair, which takes place in the Klokgebouw in Strijp-S, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, including special offers only available for attendees. You can register for free online.

“We are bringing back the large career section, expanding the number of expat centres at the fair, and growing the Family & Kids section,” says event manager Claire Leunissen.

Workshops and presentations 
The fair will also feature over 20 free workshops to help expats with job hunting, finding housing, immigration and settling advice, as well as tips on local leisure and health services, and more. The workshops have limited capacity and are filling up fast, so make sure to book seats as soon as possible — you can sign up here.

Careers and partners
The careers section includes Brainport and recruitment agency Undutchables, and offers additional advice and services for the partners of people who have moved to the region for work.

“The international community of Eindhoven can’t be underestimated,” says Claire. “Because of this small but mighty community, we are bringing the Fair back to Eindhoven to support internationals and their families looking to to settle into Dutch life as well, through career opportunities, community groups, fitness schools, Dutch classes, and more.”

Families and newcomers
New this year is a kids area, supervised by childcare provider Korein, where families can play while parents work their way round the stands.

Two international centres will be on hand for questions about registration and residency: Holland Expat Center South, based in Eindhoven, and Expat Centre Maastricht Region. Orion Immigration Law returns with a stand double the size of last year’s.

Language schools include Language Institute Regina Coeli in Vught, Una Paloma Blanca, Bart de Pau and Taalkracht, while the health and leisure exhibitors range from bike subscription service Swapfiets to Happy Bodies and Shakti Nutrition.

Every stage covered
Workshops and presentations by experts run for most of the day, covering renting, buying a house and securing a mortgage, tax, careers and schooling.

“The fair is an incredible one-stop shop for every part of life in the Netherlands,” says Claire. “International students or young professionals may initially come to the Fair looking for Dutch language classes or career opportunities, but later in life, they come to the Fair for different needs, such as preparing for retirement, buying their first home, or choosing the right daycare for their kids.”

“We are excited to bring the IamExpat Fair back to the Klokgebouw, a historic building that embodies the history of technology, innovation and immigration of Eindhoven,” says Claire.

The IamExpat Fair Eindhoven takes place in the Klokgebouw, Strijp-S on Saturday October 3 from 10am to 5pm. Entrance is free with online registration.

item.title: Dutch destinations: Move on up to Midden-Groningen
item.description:
Dutch destinations: Move on up to Midden-Groningen

August 17, 2026 Robin Pascoe

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The area of countryside known as Midden-Groningen describes itself as the “playground” of the city of the same name. The region is home to country estates, windmills, little museums and plenty of outdoor places to explore by bike, foot and by boat.

Dotted around the countryside you will also see some of the traces of the regional gas industry, which has now been shut down because of the damage caused by earthquakes.

Five things to do in Midden-Groningen

Visit a country house
The Groningen country house, or borg, Fraeylemaborg in Slochteren was lived in by its wealthy owners well into the 20th century, but parts of the complex date back to the 13th. The entire building is now open to the public, from the attic to the kitchens and offers a fascinating glimpse into the lives of wealthy Groningers.

The grounds are also open to explore and regular re-enactments are staged in the grounds. When we visited a medieval battle, complete with tents, villagers and cannon, was being re-created much to the delight of the many children in the audience. The café with its sunny terrace is a good stop for lunch.

Take in a museum
There are plenty of small, regional museums in the region. In Hoogezand you will find the national bus museum, which attracts bus fans from all over the globe, and a historic wharf that has been virtually untouched since 1922.

In Sappemeer is the fire brigade museum and your offspring will be able to help put out a fire on certain days in the summer. Zuidbroek is home to a railway museum, in the old station, with a treasure hunt, train simulator for budding drivers and a collection of model trains.

Check out a windmill 
The region is home to several windmills, some of which were used to pump out water when the land was being drained. De Wachter, on the edge of Zuidlaren, is a working oilseed mill with a small museum and great views if you can brave the ladders to reach the top.

It still produces linseed and corn oil, and four types of spices, all of which you can buy in the shop. Open on Saturday and Wednesday afternoon.

Wander in nature
The Drentsche Aa national park, on the edge of Zuidlaren, takes its name from the river Aa which meanders through the countryside from Drenthe into Groningen province. Home to plenty of wildlife and megalithic tombs known as hunebedden, it is one of the oldest landscapes in the country. You can follow various cycling and walking routes and the visitors centre has a welcoming café for lunch or high tea.

See the Veenkoloniën by boat
Pick up a canoe or an electric motorboat at Peddel en zo in Kiel-Windeweer and follow one of several routes along canals and rivers, from one hour to a full day. You will pass through ribbon villages and the remains of old peat workings, with plenty of opportunities to stop for lunch or a swim.

Where to eat
There is plenty of choice throughout the region. De Amshoff in Kiel-Windeweer comes highly recommended for dinner but was fully booked when we were there. It also offers overnight stays. Van Heijningen Bosch in Veendam is housed in a listed country house and serves lunch and evening fine dining.

The Grand Café in Zuidlaren offers traditional Dutch café fare – steaks, spare ribs – as well as cheese fondue and a hearty Dutch stew. Be aware, many places are closed Monday, Tuesday and even Wednesday, so check first.

Where to stay
We stayed in a little wooden cabin in the small-scale complex known as Romala’s Home in Kiel-Windeweer, where they also have a fascinating (enormous) shop full of bric-a-brac.

Het Torentje van Trips is a B&B in a converted water mill which sleeps up to eight in the east of the region. Zuidlaren has a couple of fairly ordinary hotels while Pieks in Noordlaren gets rave reviews online. There are also plenty of campsites if you are looking for something a little less refined.

How to get there
There are some bus and train services, but a car is probably the best, and easiest, way to get around. Rent a bike if you like cycling.

Anything else?
If you are looking for a longer stay, there is plenty more to explore in north eastern Groningen, including the fortified village of Bourtange and lots more borgs (manor houses).

item.title: Warning after Dutch blood donor infected with West Nile virus
item.description:
Warning after Dutch blood donor infected with West Nile virus

August 17, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A case of West Nile virus has been detected in a Dutch blood donor in the first infection of its kind for six years.

The donor, who lives in Utrecht province, is though to have contracted the virus in the Netherlands, as they have not been abroad recently, the public health agency RIVM said.

The virus was confirmed after the patient reported mild symptoms of West Nile fever. Blood bank Sanquin subsequently carried out laboratory tests on a number of samples.

Some 80% of people who contract the virus have no symptoms, but around 1% develop neurological problems, mainly people over 50 with weakened immune systems. In rare cases it can be fatal.

The disease mainly occurs in birds, but can be transmitted to other species, including humans, by mosquitoes. There are no known cases of transmission between humans.

Horse and bird infected

The RIVM said the virus had also been detected in a horse and a bird in different locations in the Netherlands, indicating that mosquitoes that carry the virus are active in the country.

The agency advised people to wear clothes with long sleeves, apply mosquito repellent and use screens or mosquito nets to keep the insects out. It added that the risk of contracting West Nile virus in the Netherlands was small.

item.description:
Limburg brewery’s Pils scoops top global award for second time

August 17, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Limburg brewery Alfa has won one of the top prizes at the World Beer Awards for the second time.

The family firm, based in Thull, was awarded the title of World’s Best Classic Pilsener for Edel Pils, which previously won the honour in 2021.

It was one of four Dutch beers to win a Gold award at the annual festival in the English city of Norwich, along with Grolsch’s Cal and Herfstbok and the Gouverneur Superieur Pilsener made by another Limburg brewery, Lindeboom.

Edel Pils was also named as the best Dutch national beer by the international jury.

Alfa has been brewing beer in Thull for 156 years, using traditional family recipes and its own water source.

item.title: Dutch companies to receive €1bn in Trump tariff compensation
item.description:
Dutch companies to receive €1bn in Trump tariff compensation

August 17, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch companies are set to recoup a €1 billion windfall from the Trump administration after the United States Supreme Court ruled most of his “liberation day” tariffs announced last April were illegal.

Philips, one of the first companies to claim a refund following the ruling in February, received €186 mln, which accounted for around 4% of its turnover for the second quarter of 2026.

The figures were included in the health tech giant’s latest quarterly results, which showed a 4% increase in sales compared to the same period in 2025.

The Supreme Court ordered the US government to compensate companies when it upheld a lower court’s decision that the Trump administration had wrongly used emergency powers to justify the tariffs.

Exactly how much has been paid out is unknown because the government has not published details, but experts have calculated that the top 10 Dutch exporters stand to receive more than €1 bn altogether.

Philips, which makes 40% of its turnover in North America, was one of the first Dutch companies to claim a refund. Other major exporters include Heineken, which is expected to receive between €150 mln and €350 mln, and Ahold Delaize, owner of Albert Heijn, which will get an estimated €100 mln to €300 million.

Altogether more than a quarter of a million companies have claimed refunds worth a total of $129 bn (€111 bn) from the US customs administration, in addition to the $166 bn (€143 bn) which will have to be repaid to American firms.

“We are surprised by how quickly and efficiently this has happened,” Casper Roerade of Dutch entrepreneurs’ association EvoFenedex told AD.nl.

item.title: Far-right FVD-linked school opens in Almere with state funding
item.description:
Far-right FVD-linked school opens in Almere with state funding

August 17, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A primary school linked to the far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD) has opened with state funding in Almere, teaching pupils that “the old Europe was better than the new,” and doing away with the “dogma of equality”.

The “Renaissance School” started with one class of 18 four and five-year-olds. Its founders say the curriculum follows the view of humanity found in classical antiquity, the middle ages and the early modern period.

The school’s site says it approaches scientific views such as climate change as “falsifiable theories” and that boys and girls may be taught differently in recognition of biological differences, NRC reported.

School head Douwe Filz told De Telegraaf that classes are mixed and there are no separate subjects for boys or girls, although material may be presented in different ways.

Pupils are taught Latin and English alongside Dutch, and the school works with printed books, has no wifi and makes limited use of computers.

FVD has presented its Renaissance schools as an answer to what it calls left-wing indoctrination in the classroom, a theme it has pursued since setting up a reporting hotline for pupils in 2019. Ralf Dekker, who led the project for the party, told NOS in 2022 there would be “no woke thinking in the teaching material”.

The school is run by Stichting Tocqueville, formally separate from FVD, although several of its board members and staff are active in the party. Party chairman Thierry Baudet has described it as part of an FVD pillar alongside the party itself.

Questions in parliament
VVD MP Arend Kisteman and D66 MP Ilana Rooderkerk have written parliamentary questions about the school, which will be answered when parliament reconvenes after August 31.

“It is too easy to set up a small school in the Netherlands,” Kisteman told De Telegraaf. “That worsens the teacher shortage and the taxpayer picks up the bill.”

Rooderkerk told the paper she wanted inspectors to step in before four-year-olds were indoctrinated with FVD’s ideas. Judith Tielen, the VVD junior education minister, is drawing up options for tightening the rules and said inspectors would carry out a full quality inspection within the school’s first year.

The Dutch constitution has allowed publicly funded faith and worldview schools since 1917. Most of those founded since a 2020 law relaxed the rules are faith schools, the biggest share of them are Islamic.

Market research tactics
Schools seeking state funding normally have to collect 100 signed declarations from parents, which FVD failed to do.

Instead, the school’s backers used market research to show that the population of the area will increase, boosting the need for a new school.

An earlier attempt to open the Renaissance School in Almere, which was fully funded by parents and private sources, failed and closed in 2024.
